passages.t: Who will stand surety for him?
passages.happening:
“My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; the grave awaits me” (verse 1). Mockers surround him.

Then a plea to God: “Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand. Who else will be my guarantor?” (verse 3). God has closed the friends' minds to understanding.

“He has made me a byword among the people, a man in whose face they spit. My eyes have grown dim with grief, and my whole body is but a shadow” (verses 6-7). Yet he says the upright are appalled at what they see, and then, as if to steady himself: “Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 16 rose to Job's witness in heaven. Chapter 17 finishes the same speech, and it sinks again. That rise and fall is typical of Job's speeches in the middle of the book: a moment of daring hope, followed by exhaustion and gloom. But the thread of hope is not cut.

The picture in verse 3 comes from ancient business and law. When someone took on a debt, another could stand as guarantor, promising to pay if the first failed, and the promise was sealed in public by striking hands. Proverbs warns against doing it rashly, which shows how common and how risky it was. No one will stand surety for Job. So he asks God to lay down the pledge for him, the same paradox as chapter 16: he appeals to God against the charges he feels God is bringing.

A byword was a name that became proverbial as an example of disaster, and in popular thinking it was a sign of divine punishment. Spitting in someone's face was extreme contempt. Job suffers not only in body but in reputation, and the Bible treats public shame as a real and deep suffering.
passages.later: Judah stood surety in the same way for his brother Benjamin: “I will guarantee his safety. You may hold me personally responsible” (Genesis 43:9).
passages.asks: Job had no one to stand surety for him. Ask who has stood up for you when you could not stand up for yourself. And ask whose name has become a byword in your circle, and whether you have joined in.

passages.happening:
“But come back and try again, all of you. For I will not find a wise man among you” (verse 10).

His days are past, his plans broken off. The friends say light is near, but it is darkness. If he looks for Sheol as his home, spreads his bed in the dark, and calls the pit his father and the worm his mother or sister, ‘where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?’ (verse 15).

“Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Verse 12 is obscure in Hebrew. It probably means that the friends keep promising light while Job sees only night.

Verse 14 uses family words for death. Calling decay his father and the worm his mother or sister means treating the grave as his closest kin, the household he is about to join. For a man whose children are dead and whose relatives have turned away, the picture is desolate: the only family left to welcome him is the grave.

The chapter ends with a question, and the question is about hope, tiqvah, used twice in verse 15. It echoes chapter 14, where Job said that God destroys a man's hope.
passages.hard:
Has Job given up hope by the end of this chapter?

Some readers take this as the low point of Job's faith, a moment when he expects nothing from God. Others point out that the chapter still holds signs of hope. In verse 3 Job appeals to God to be his guarantor, and in verse 9 he affirms that the righteous hold to their way and grow stronger. His questions are asked of God and before God, not in giving him up.

A common reading is that Job has lost hope in anything he can see, including recovery in this life, but has not stopped reaching toward God. Chapter 19 supports it, where the same man says that his Redeemer lives. Job's darkness here is real, and it is not the end of his story.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job asked where his hope was, and he kept asking God. Ask where your hope is today, honestly. And ask whether you are still asking God, even if the answer has not come.
